passage: I'm Salma, and I sat next to Samir on his last day before moving to another office. Samir spent the final hour typing a handoff for the supplier contract renewal: four lines. "Renewal due end of month. Contact is R. Nair. Prices in the shared file." Samir closed the laptop, smiling. I did not say anything; I was not the one receiving it. But I knew that the last supplier call had gone badly, and that the price in the file was one Samir had agreed verbally. None of that was in the note. Two weeks later the new person phoned the supplier and was quoted a higher price. I wonder if Samir simply thought it was obvious.

qa.q: What did the handoff note say about the contact?
qa.a: The note said the contact is R. Nair.

qa.q: What might Samir have been feeling when closing the laptop, smiling?
qa.a: Relieved and satisfied, believing the four-line note covered everything.

qa.q: What could Samir have added before leaving?
qa.a: The background of the last supplier call, the price agreed verbally and any risks, or a short walkthrough call.

qa.q: How might the new person have felt on being quoted a higher price?
qa.a: Surprised and stuck, with no background to explain the gap, through no fault of their own.

grounding: Shows a worker leaving a task with a brief note, assuming the successor knows the background that only lived in memory.

passage:
Friday. Akash was moving to a new team on Monday and wrote a short note for Pema about the annual fair booking: "Stalls booked. Sound system pending. Ask the caretaker." He signed off, glad to be done.

Tuesday. Pema sent three messages: which sound company? What is the caretaker's number? Was a deposit paid? Akash, busy in the new team, replied with one word: "Later."

Next Friday. The sound company had not been paid and cancelled the slot. Pema found the invoice in Akash's old email. Hearing about it, Akash sat quietly. "I knew all that. I just didn't write it down."

qa.q: What did Akash's note say about the sound system?
qa.a: The note said: "Sound system pending."

qa.q: What might Akash have felt when saying "I knew all that. I just didn't write it down"?
qa.a: Regretful and a bit ashamed, realising that what was known in his head had not travelled.

qa.q: What could Akash have done on the Friday before leaving?
qa.a: Write down which sound company, the deposit, the caretaker's number and the deadline, and offer a short call.

qa.q: How might Pema have felt on finding the cancelled slot?
qa.a: Frustrated and stressed, having had to reconstruct facts without background and lost the booking anyway.

grounding: Shows a worker who hands over a task with a brief note, assuming the successor knows the reasons and details.

passage:
On her last day in the Istanbul office, Zeynep handed the monthly supplier report to Kaito. She was moving to the new project team the next morning. Her note said: "Same as usual. Pull the numbers on the 3rd, check Ankara, send to finance by the 5th."
Check Ankara. To Zeynep, that meant something obvious: the Ankara depot counted returns twice, and she always subtracted them by hand. She had done it for two years. It was so automatic she didn't think of it as knowledge.
Kaito, who had never done the report, checked that the Ankara numbers were there. They were. He sent it on the 5th.
On the 9th, the finance manager called Zeynep. The supplier totals were much too high. Zeynep's stomach sank as she realised. She walked over to Kaito's desk. "I'm sorry," she said. "That was my fault, not yours. Let me show you the Ankara thing properly."

qa.q: What did Zeynep's note say to check?
qa.a: Check Ankara.

qa.q: How did Zeynep feel when the finance manager called?
qa.a: Zeynep felt a sinking guilt, realising the Ankara correction had lived only in her head.

qa.q: What could Zeynep's handover note have included?
qa.a: The reason behind "check Ankara": that the depot counts returns twice and the returns must be subtracted by hand.

qa.q: How might Kaito have felt when the totals were wrong?
qa.a: Kaito might have felt confused and worried he had failed, though he had done exactly what the note said.

grounding: Illustrates a worker who hands over a task with a brief note, assuming the successor knows background that lived only in her head.

passage:
In the staff room of Greenfield School, Ojas left a note on the Class Eight science register before his two-week leave: "Chapter 6 next. Lab project pending. Amandeep, all yours. Thanks!"
Amandeep, who taught the other section, took the class on Monday. "Lab project pending" meant, to her, that it hadn't been set. She set it: a plant-growth experiment, due in two weeks.
Half the class groaned. A girl in the front said, "Ma'am, we already submitted it to Ojas sir last week." Others hadn't. Nobody knew which. The register didn't say.
Amandeep spent her free period and lunch going desk by desk, asking. Three students had lost their work in the confusion.
When Ojas called in on Wednesday and heard, he was quiet for a moment. "I knew exactly who had submitted. It was all in my head. I should have written the list." That evening he emailed her the names, with an apology.

qa.q: What did Ojas's note say about the lab project?
qa.a: Lab project pending.

qa.q: How did Ojas feel when he heard what had happened?
qa.a: Ojas felt guilty and regretful, going quiet and admitting the list had been only in his head.

qa.q: What would have made the note useful?
qa.a: Stating who had already submitted the project and who hadn't, instead of just "pending."

qa.q: What was Monday like for Amandeep?
qa.a: Amandeep was confused and pressured, spending her free period and lunch asking desk by desk to rebuild what the note left out.

grounding: Shows a teacher who hands over a class with a brief note, assuming his colleague knows what he knows, and the confusion that follows.

passage:
Hi Gopika,
I'm so sorry about this week. You shouldn't have had to deal with it.
When I handed over the café's supplier orders, I wrote "Order as usual, list is on the board." I thought that covered it. It didn't cover the things I had just stopped noticing: that the dairy supplier needs a call on Tuesday, not a message, or he doesn't deliver on Thursday; that the bread order doubles on weekends; that we switched coffee beans last month and the old code still sits on the board.
So on Thursday you had no milk, too little bread on Saturday, and the wrong coffee arrived. And the customers blamed you.
I've written it all down properly now, attached below: what's ordered, when, how, and who to call if something goes wrong. Can we do a fifteen-minute call tomorrow so I can walk you through it?
Kiran

qa.q: What did Kiran's original note say?
qa.a: Order as usual, list is on the board.

qa.q: How does Kiran feel about the handover now?
qa.a: Kiran feels sorry and guilty that Gopika had to deal with problems caused by missing information.

qa.q: What does Kiran do now to fix the handover?
qa.a: Kiran writes down what is ordered, when, how and who to call, and offers a fifteen-minute call to walk Gopika through it.

qa.q: What was the week like for Gopika?
qa.a: Gopika faced no milk, too little bread and the wrong coffee, and customers blamed Gopika for gaps that were not Gopika's fault.

grounding: Illustrates a worker whose brief handover note leaves out knowledge that lived in the head, and who later writes it down properly.

passage: So, Ishita, you want to know why I now write handoff notes like essays? Okay. Last year, before my two weeks of leave, I passed the supply-order tracker at the clinic to Arun. My note said: "Check sheet, send reminders Friday, the usual." Three lines. I, Ayesha, the organised one, thought it was obvious. What I didn't write: that one supplier must be reminded by phone, never email, because their inbox is broken. That the red rows meant "on hold, don't chase". That the Friday reminder skips the clinic's own lab. All of that lived in my head; I'd done it for a year. So Arun emailed the broken inbox, chased every red row, and reminded our own lab. Nothing dangerous happened, but I came back to three annoyed people and one very apologetic Arun, who had done exactly what my note said.

qa.q: How many lines was Ayesha's handoff note?
qa.a: Three lines.

qa.q: What was Ayesha feeling when writing the note, and how did that change after the leave?
qa.a: Ayesha felt confident and sure it was obvious after doing the job for a year, then embarrassed on coming back to three annoyed people.

qa.q: What could Ayesha have added to the handoff?
qa.a: The phone-only supplier, what the red rows meant and that the Friday reminder skips the lab, plus a short talk-through with Arun before leaving.

qa.q: How might Arun have felt while covering the tracker?
qa.a: Arun likely felt confused and then sorry, since following the note exactly still caused trouble through no fault of Arun's own.

grounding: Shows a worker handing over a task with a brief note, assuming the successor knows background that lived only in their head.
